analysis.one_liner: Ends a federal tax deduction for hardrock mines operating on public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have repealed the percentage depletion tax break for hardrock mines on public lands, died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Hardrock mining companies that take gold, silver, copper, and other metals from public land can claim a "percentage depletion" deduction, which lets them shave a set percentage of their gross income off their taxable income every year, on top of deducting what they actually spent. Critics call this a double subsidy because the miners already get the minerals themselves at little or no charge under the 1872 general mining law. This bill would have denied that deduction for hardrock mines on public lands or on land patented under those laws, effective for tax years after 1996.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who would collect more revenue because hardrock miners on public land could no longer deduct a percentage of their gross income. The effect would fall on mining companies extracting gold, silver, copper, and similar metals from federal land.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Internal Revenue Code to disallow the percentage depletion allowance for hardrock mines located on land subject to the general mining laws or patented under them, ending a tax deduction these companies otherwise claim.

The bill's title frames the deduction as a double subsidy, since companies already obtain hardrock minerals from public land cheaply under the general mining laws and then take a percentage-of-income tax deduction on top of it.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on public lands, which would owe more federal income tax once they lost the percentage depletion deduction.

drawbacks.text: The bill applied only to hardrock mines tied to the general mining laws, leaving depletion deductions for mines on private or other lands untouched, so the subsidy would have survived in some places.

Repealing a long-standing deduction raises costs for a domestic mining industry, which supporters of the allowance have traditionally argued could affect mining jobs and the competitiveness of U.S. producers against foreign mines; the bill text and summary do not address this concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy is narrow but straightforward: close one tax deduction for one group of companies, raising revenue at the expense of an industry that already receives minerals from public land at little cost. The main honest objection is the competitive burden on domestic miners, and the bill does nothing to address the broader 1872 mining law itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Dale Bumpers introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, joined by original cosponsors Senators Feingold, Leahy, and Kohl, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 105th Congress, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies on public land kept the percentage depletion tax deduction, and taxpayers continued to forgo that revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies kept the tax break

for.name: Sen. Dale Bumpers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the percentage depletion allowance for hardrock mines on public lands.

for.name: Sens. Feingold, Leahy, and Kohl
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Two additional senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it five cosponsors total: four Democrats and one Republican.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan backing at five cosponsors (four Democrats and one Republican), but no senator is recorded as opposing it either; it simply never moved in committee.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies on public lands
industries.note: The bill would have ended their percentage depletion deduction, raising their federal income taxes. Their gain from the bill's failure is revenue the public forgoes, on top of minerals they already take from public land cheaply under the 1872 mining law.
